message.content:
**Los Angeles (Pacific Time) vs. Berlin (Central European Time)**  

| Period | Los Angeles | Berlin | Time‑zone offset | Difference |
|--------|-------------|--------|------------------|------------|
| **Standard Time** (winter) | UTC‑8 | UTC+1 | 9 hours ahead | **+9 h** |
| **Daylight Saving Time** (summer) | UTC‑7 | UTC+2 | 9 hours ahead | **+9 h** |
| **Transition windows** | | | | |
| Early March (after US DST starts, before EU DST starts) | UTC‑7 | UTC+1 | 8 hours ahead | **+8 h** |
| Late October (after EU DST ends, before US DST ends) | UTC‑7 | UTC+1 | 8 hours ahead | **+8 h** |

### How it works

| Region | DST start | DST end | Offset during DST |
|--------|-----------|---------|-------------------|
| **United States (Los Angeles)** | 2nd Sunday in March | 1st Sunday in November | UTC‑7 |
| **European Union (Berlin)** | Last Sunday in March | Last Sunday in October | UTC+2 |

Because the start and end dates don’t line up exactly, there are two short windows each year (late March and late October) when the two cities are **8 hours apart** instead of the usual **9 hours**.

### Quick examples (current year)

| Date | Los Angeles | Berlin | Difference |
|------|-------------|--------|------------|
| 15 March | 10 AM PT | 7 PM CET | +9 h |
| 20 March | 10 AM PDT | 7 PM CET | +8 h |
| 15 October | 10 AM PDT | 7 PM CEST | +8 h |
| 20 October | 10 AM PDT | 7 PM CEST | +9 h |

> **Tip:** If you’re scheduling across time zones, double‑check the DST dates for the year in question to avoid the 8‑hour overlap.
